articles.title: 3 Iranian-backed men indicted in attempted plot on RAF Fairford
articles.snippet: Three men, with one working from jail, allegedly conspired to commit around 20 terrorist attacks across the U.S. and Europe, including the plot on RAF Fairford, on behalf of Iran-aligned terrorist networks.
articles.full_text:
Federal prosecutors allege that an Iranian terrorist proxy group’s commander, alongside two other men, assisted in orchestrating the suspected terror plot on a United Kingdom military base from jail while awaiting trial on other pending terrorism charges.
From jail in New York, Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, allegedly coordinated with Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iraqi and Iranian national, respectively, to organize the recent failed terror attack on RAF Fairford, according to a recent Department of Justice release.
The three men allegedly conspired to commit nearly 20 terrorist attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the U.S. in the name of two Iran-aligned terrorist networks that are designated by the U.S. as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, per an eight-count indictment.
“Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of New York said in the release. “The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real.”
The indictment says that most recently, al-Hassani, with terrorism-related offenses for their activities in support of Kataib Hezbollah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, allegedly managed the September plot on RAF Fairford, which housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel at the time in support of the war in Iran.
In the Southern District of New York, al-Saadi was in jail awaiting trial on pending terrorism charges and tried to correspond with al-Hassani and Mohajeri by passing coded messages through third parties. Al-Hassani and Mohajeri were both in Iran at the time of the attempted RAF Fairford scheme, so they relied on a network of contacts in the U.K., per the statement.
Al-Saadi was charged in May for collaborating with and working on behalf of the IRGC, other FTOs and Kataib Hezbollah, an Iraqi militia group that he is the commander of and that is backed by the IRGC. He was also charged for his participation in planning and promoting around 18 terrorist attacks in Europe and for attempting to bomb a synagogue in New York.
The indictment alleges that al-Hassani and Mohajeri, an operative of the IRGC, worked with al-Saadi to facilitate and complete many of the European terrorist attacks. Al-Hassani used his contacts and criminal associates to carry out attacks in the U.K., prosecutors allege.
Al-Saadi was arrested abroad in early May and transferred to U.S. custody for prosecution, staying in federal custody since his arrival in the U.S. For four months following his arrest, there were no additional attacks attributed to the three men.
Then in August, prosecutors say that al-Hassani directed and paid associates in the U.K. to conduct “preparatory steps” for the RAF Fairford plot, such as surveillance of the base’s perimeter. The next month, he also paid several people to assist in the plot’s preparation, like procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching chemical accelerants and purchasing items that could be used as explosive shrapnel.
In late September, al-Hassani supposedly told individuals to drive three vans, some with barrels of fuel inside, to RAF Fairford, but at least two encountered a security roadblock and were not able to continue to the base. U.K. law enforcement authorities later recovered three white vans and arrested the individuals.
While in jail, al-Saadi allegedly used phone calls with his family in Iraq to pass coded messages to al-Hassani and Mohajeri in the days leading up to the RAF Fairford plot. Three days before the attempted plot, al-Saadi spoke with his family on the phone and inquired about how al-Hassani was doing, telling them to give him money so “we can do it.”
The eight-count indictment lists six charges for all three with a total maximum penalty of 90 years in prison or life in prison, and two charges reserved only for al-Saadi, with a maximum of 20 years or life in prison.

articles.title: Finland says it detects strike on Russian warship in Baltic Sea
articles.snippet: Finland's military said on Thursday its forces had detected "a strike" on a Russian warship in the Baltic Sea a day earlier, but that the security situation in the area remained stable.
articles.full_text:
HELSINKI — Finland’s military said on Thursday its forces had detected “a strike” on a Russian warship in the Baltic Sea a day earlier, but that the security situation in the area remained stable.
It was not immediately clear if there were any casualties or what had caused the strike. Estonian media reported on Thursday that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship and that it later returned to St. Petersburg.
“The Finnish Defence Forces detected… a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation,” a spokesperson for the Nordic country’s military said in an emailed statement to Reuters.
Finland is not under any immediate military threat, the spokesperson added. The defense forces declined to provide further details about the location or timing of the incident, or how it was detected.
Ukraine has been sending waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwest Leningrad region, which includes the city of St. Petersburg as well as the Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga, a major export outlet for commodities such as oil and grain.
Some Ukrainian drones have strayed into the airspace of Finland and the Baltic region, leading to fears that the war is spilling over into NATO countries that border Russia and its ally Belarus.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania early on Wednesday issued warnings to citizens to take shelter due to drones in their airspace, and NATO scrambled warplanes in response.
The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia that extends eastwards to St Petersburg.

articles.title: Guard appears to rebuke Hegseth’s delegation at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
articles.snippet: The U.S. Army sentinel moved toward the group and, from a distance, shouted toward them: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
articles.full_text:
A U.S. Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier appeared to rebuke Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth‘s delegation on Wednesday after laughter could be heard as they climbed the steps of the solemn site, according to a video of the incident.
Hegseth, his wife and senior aides could be seen taking pictures and speaking to each other on the steps of the memorial at Arlington National Cemetery following a Veterans Day event.
Immediately after the laughter, the sentinel moved toward the group and, from a distance, shouted toward them: “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”
Sitting at the heart of Arlington National Cemetery, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is a sacred site and the grave of three unknown American service members, including one from World War I. It is widely known as a place for mourning and for reflection on military service, and sentinels guard the site 24 hours a day.
Asked about the incident, which was first reported by CNN, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement: “The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored — and will always honor — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe.”
“While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum,” Parnell said.
Hegseth, a former Army National Guard soldier who served in Iraq, prevailed this week after the House of Representatives rejected a Republican lawmaker’s effort to impeach him.
At a rare Pentagon press conference on Tuesday hours before the vote, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a farce and defended his record, which includes championing the unpopular Iran war, launching strikes on suspected drug vessels in Latin American waters and firing senior military officers.
Democrats who won control of both chambers of Congress last week have promised to investigate Hegseth for his stewardship of the U.S. military and have not ruled out another impeachment effort.

articles.title: Inside Warhound’s plan to engineer a better military working dog
articles.snippet: The company plans to clone top-performing dogs, edit genes associated with health problems and introduce standardized training to puppies as young as two weeks old.
articles.full_text:
News broke on Oct. 22 that a new startup had raised $200 million to genetically enhance military dogs. The company, Warhound, was launched by billionaire entrepreneurs Ben Lamm, founder of biotech company Colossal Biosciences, and Palmer Luckey, founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries.
The two planned to bring their respective companies’ strengths to the venture. Lamm would apply Colossal’s gene-editing technology to improve the dogs’ physical capabilities, while Luckey would equip them with advanced military equipment. The unusual mission, combined with the founders’ track records, left plenty of questions about what Warhound had planned.
Some speculated that the company intended to create cybernetic superdogs, while others accused its founders of trying to expand an industry that should instead be replaced with robots. But in a news release shared in response to the initial reporting, Warhound described a more grounded goal: rebuilding the domestic supply of dogs for the military, law enforcement and first responders.
In an interview with Military Times, Lamm and Warhound’s co-founder and chief executive David Spirk, who left a senior position at Palantir for the startup, expanded on that statement, discussing the conversations that sparked the mission, the problems they want to address and the product they hope to sell.
Together, they said they want to do more than bring the supply chain to the United States. Their plan includes cloning top-performing dogs, editing genes associated with health problems and introducing standardized training to puppies as young as two weeks old.
A meeting of minds
The idea for Warhound was born out of conversations Lamm had with Luckey beginning around April 2025. They had met at the Moonshots Summit, where they appeared as guest speakers.
“Palmer’s really excited about animals, and he knows I run both the extinction and species conservation company. So, we’re talking about all kinds of stuff, like can you communicate with animals, all these things leveraging technology, and then he started talking to me about the working dog program,” Lamm said.
According to the Defense Department, only about 13% of the dogs trained to become military working dogs come from domestic breeders. Conversely, Warhound estimates that around 80% of the dogs are sourced from overseas, mostly Europe. Lamm described those breeding programs as “a little bit puppy millish.”
Because of supply issues and the time it takes to train a working dog, Warhound estimates that it takes roughly three years before a dog becomes operational. The company said more than half the dogs procured are ultimately deemed unfit for service, meaning the government has to “train roughly 200 dogs today to field 100 working animals tomorrow.”
To address the problem, Lamm said his conversations with Luckey over the past 18 months have evolved from identifying the problem to figuring out how technology could help solve it.
“[Luckey] thought that Anduril could provide a lot of the tech and enabled hardware around this,” Lamm said. “And we could provide the cloning and the genetic engineering.”
The science behind Warhound
Since launching in 2021, Colossal has raised more than $435 million to fund its efforts to revive extinct animals and conserve the genetic material of endangered species. The company’s current valuation is approximately $10.2 billion.
To expand its capabilities, Colossal acquired Texas-based Viagen Pets and Equine last year. Lamm said Viagen has “very high cloning efficiencies … and Warhound will be leveraging Viagen as it relates to dog cloning, which is their core business.”
In 2025, Colossal demonstrated its capabilities by cloning former NFL quarterback Tom Brady’s dog. But cloning and gene editing are distinct processes.
According to the National Institutes of Health, cloning produces a genetically identical copy of an existing animal, whereas gene editing involves directly altering an organism’s DNA to change specific characteristics.
With gene editing, “you’re taking the random chance out of nature,” Lamm said, adding, “Genetic engineering is looking at the genome, finding things that are broken in the genome, wrong in the genome, or could lead to health consequences, and fixing and removing that.”
Gene editing has been used to create specific characteristics in several animal species. Scientists, for example, have used the technique to make pigs more resistant to certain diseases; cattle better suited for hotter environments; and fish grow faster. But its application in dogs remains limited.
In August, the company Kindred Companion Sciences unveiled what it described as the first genetically edited dogs. The biotech company created two hypoallergenic beagles using gene editing to remove a DNA sequence associated with a major dog allergen.
However, Lamm said he does not anticipate significant challenges to applying the technology to working dogs.
“We’re working on stuff that’s like a hundred times more advanced than, you know, a couple dog edits,” he said, referring to his team at Colossal.
“When we made our dire wolves, we made 20 edits, which included edits specifically from dire wolves in those variants that had not existed for over 12,000 years in the genome, so not only can we make edits, but we can even make edits with lost alleles,” he added.
Engineering a better working dog
While the science might not be a problem, Warhound co-founder Spirk said the company’s immediate focus is identifying “the best of the best” dogs and breeds to biobank, as well as developing the company’s “Warhound standard” for training working dogs.
He explained that a wide variety of dogs are used across federal, regional and local agencies. Warhound is working with different government organizations to identify the top-performing animals, though he declined to say which ones.
He said they are “understanding who wants what type of dog, and what the specialized capabilities of that dog are.”
“You can imagine that the dog that we need sitting outside McDill Air Force Base is much different than a dog that somebody’s going to jump out of a helicopter with,” Spirk continued.
Using genetic material collected in the biobank, Warhound scientists will map the animals’ genomes and look for opportunities to edit genes to improve their overall health, wellness and longevity before beginning the cloning process.
“Once the scientists do their magic and make these dogs, we will immediately begin training,” Spirk said, adding that their experts suggest training should begin for puppies as young as two weeks.
The idea behind early training, he explained, is to breed dogs to the highest standard, and then begin acclimating them to the tasks and conditions they’ll be expected to encounter in the field. For example, he said, a dog trained primarily on asphalt might struggle to function on a different surface, such as grass or sand.
“You’re just naturally going to have a better product coming out when we domesticate the production,” Spirk said.
The first Warhounds should be “coming off the line” in about two years, he said.
Once Warhound figures out the right balance of nature and nurture for working dogs, Spirk said the company would like to explore ways to apply its research to the other 98 million dogs in America.
“Nobody’s ever had the resources to do it and to figure it out,” he said, adding, “It’s pretty motivating.”

articles.title: Romanian servers targeted by Russian hackers to scoop up emails about NATO, EU
articles.snippet: Hackers linked to Russia's FSB quietly compromised a Romanian government organization’s servers to collect emails related to NATO and the EU in December 2025, a Slovak cybersecurity firm has revealed.
articles.full_text:
VIENNA — Hackers linked to Russia’s FSB quietly compromised a Romanian government organization’s servers to collect emails related to NATO and the EU in December 2025, a Slovak cybersecurity firm has revealed.
Using an advanced suite of tools that the researchers dubbed Cereal, a pun on the technology of serialization, emails going through Romanian government servers were scanned for a relation to NATO and the European Union. If this was discovered, the malicious software would create a copy for its Russian spymasters.
In particular, one component, CerealBox, targeted messages involving NATO and EU institutional addresses, the cybersecurity form ESET said. The module selected emails with Word or PDF attachments using predefined filters, then compressed and encrypted copies for later retrieval by the attackers.
The hack was discovered by the Bratislava-based company and made public on Nov. 10. ESET had first discovered the tool being used against Kazakhstan in November 2025, and found the infiltration of Romania’s Microsoft Exchange servers a month later.
In a blog post and press release, the company attributed the attack to the known hacking group Turla, which it said was generally considered to be affiliated with Russia’s FSB, the country’s domestic intelligence agency. Turla has also been involved in attacks against high-profile Ukrainian targets, and the researchers said 70% of countries the group targeted were post-Soviet or post-communist states in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The APT – a term designating an “Advanced Persistent Threat,” or known hacking group – primarily attacks government institutions.
ESET attributed the toolset to Turla with high confidence, citing the simultaneous use of another component publicly linked to the group and conceptual similarities to older Turla malware.
The researchers also noted a surge in activity in Kazakhstan on Jan. 15, 2026, the day after Old New Year, an informal holiday observed in Russia and some neighboring countries. “While malware does not celebrate holidays, its operators do,” the company wrote.
Romanian servers were compromised on Dec. 23, 2025, ESET researchers said; roughly a month after the cybersecurity firm first detected the same malicious code on the server of a Kazakh government agency. That discovery was the first time this tool had been seen, which the researchers described as “a previously undocumented toolset: a collection of modular .NET malware designed to run on Microsoft Exchange servers, receive commands, execute them in memory, map the compromised organization, and collect selected email messages.”
The tool was unusual for its “combination of novel techniques requiring deep knowledge of Exchange internals with unusual .NET execution methods,” ESET wrote.
The tool was designed to be especially stealthy, meant to allow it to spy undetected at length. While malware commonly communicates with an external command-and-control server, which can lead to detection and help cybersecurity professionals trace the origin, Cereal used the target organization’s own Microsoft servers as its infrastructure.
Romania is an eastern flank member of NATO and has faced physical and digital spillover of the confrontation between Russia and the West, particularly since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. Airspace violations, drone shootdowns and even the strike of commercial vessels in its exclusive economic zone have been among the consequences.
The country has also been targeted by cyber warfare. In May 2025, another known Russian APT actor attacked arms makers involved in supporting Ukraine, including those located in Romania; and just months after the war broke out, government websites were hit by a crude distributed denial-of-service attack, making Romanian public-authority and financial-sector websites unavailable for several hours.

articles.title: House Republicans sidestep effort to impeach Hegseth
articles.snippet: In a 211 to 204 vote, House Republicans sent proposed impeachment articles against Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, quashing the effort.
articles.full_text:
The House voted Tuesday evening to send the proposed impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the House Judiciary Committee, effectively quashing an effort to oust Hegseth from his cabinet post.
In a 211 to 204 vote, House Republicans sidestepped an effort proposed by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky to impeach Hegseth. Massie charged that Hegseth was negligent and conducted illegal activity in his handling of counternarcotics operations and extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean and Pacific; attacking Iran in February without congressional approval; retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for the veteran lawmaker’s statements to troops on illegal orders; capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro without a declaration of war; and other operations.
“Secretary of Defense Peter Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law,” the articles stated.
The decision to send the articles to the Judiciary Committee likely delays the vote until January, when Democrats take over the majority in Congress.
As of Thursday, Democrats won 256 seats in the House to the Republicans’ 168, while in the Senate, Democrats have at least 54 seats to 44 Republican seats.
If the House votes to impeach Hegseth next year, a two-thirds majority would be needed on any of the articles to force Hegseth out of office.
In a rare news conference Tuesday morning before the vote, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” seeking to “do damage to this president, this country, and most irresponsibly, the warriors who defend it.”
Noting that President Donald Trump was impeached twice but not convicted, Hegseth said he would “take that company every day of the week.”
“These resolutions are a farce. They mock the Constitution. They attack the chain of command, and they criminalize the warfighters who execute lawful orders,” Hegseth said.
Trump has said he would stand by his defense secretary, saying Monday that he’s “done a very good job.”
If the effort had succeeded, it would have marked the second impeachment of a U.S. defense secretary and third of a cabinet member. In 2024, Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached over President Joe Biden’s immigration policies at the U.S.-Mexico border. The Senate voted to dismiss the charges before it went to trial.
Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached in 1876 on corruption charges shortly after he resigned. He was later acquitted in the Senate.
A survey released in October by the military-veterans advocacy non-profit Common Defense found that troops and family members are uncomfortable with what they see as the politicization of the armed forces.
According to the survey, conducted by Change Research, 54% of active-duty personnel surveyed disapproved of Hegseth, while 64% of military family members disapproved.
A majority of the group of 731 active-duty troops, veterans and military family members also believe decisions within the department were being made for political gain, and 53% of active-duty personnel said the politicization was making them want to leave the military sooner than anticipated.
Nearly half the active-duty personnel also said they oppose Operation Epic Fury, the United States’ operation against Iran.

articles.title: US soldier arrested in UK for suspected ‘espionage’ for Russia
articles.snippet: A senior U.S. soldier was arrested in Britain on suspicion of assisting Russian ​intelligence, British police said on Tuesday.
articles.full_text:
A senior U.S. soldier was arrested in Britain on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence, British police said on Tuesday, after the U.S. removed aircraft from British military bases over a separate apparent threat from Iran.
FBI Director Kash Patel said the arrest of the 41-year-old man was related to “allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”
Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, added: “The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”
The arrest, which took place near the city of Gloucester, west England, on Tuesday, “is not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations,” British police said.
But it occurred the day after the U.S. removed refuelling aircraft from a British airbase in the second such apparent evacuation in three months.
Planes left the Royal Air Force base in Mildenhall, eastern England, on Monday, which, according to the Wall Street Journal, was prompted by a threat from Iran.
The U.S. in September withdrew bombers that had been used to strike Iran from RAF Fairford on security grounds over an incident police have linked to Iran, which has denied any links to attacks or incidents in Britain.
The soldier arrested on Tuesday was detained on suspicion of offenses under sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service. Police said the country to which the allegations relate is Russia.

articles.title: AUKUS on track, even ‘ahead of schedule’ for some parts, admiral says
articles.snippet: The USS Colorado will serve as the first submarine assigned to Submarine Rotational Force-West in support of AUKUS Pillar I.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The US, United Kingdom and Australia are on schedule — and even further along than expected in some aspects — in implementing the trilateral AUKUS agreement established in 2021, the commander of Submarine Forces for the US Pacific Fleet said today.
“The most consequential allied initiative is AUKUS, which is on plan and in several areas ahead of schedule,” Rear Adm. Chris Cavanaugh said during the Submarine League Annual Symposium. “I see progress in AUKUS every day.”
The trilateral deal comprises Pillar I, which is focused on providing Australia with Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarines by 2032, and Pillar II, where the nations are working together to jointly develop and field advanced military capabilities.
It’s not clear which areas of AUKUS are ahead of schedule. However, Cavanaugh pointed to the reactivation of Submarine Squadron 3 in the spring in support of standing up Submarine Rotational Force-West (SRF-West) based out of Royal Australian Navy base HMAS Stirling as evidence of progress on the AUKUS deal. Establishing SRF-West is a Pillar I priority enabling the US and the UK to provide a rotational presence of nuclear-powered fast-attack submarines — up to four from the US and one from the UK — at HMAS Stirling.
Further, the three countries announced in October that the US’s Virginia-class submarine Colorado would serve as the first submarine assigned to SRF-West, starting late next year. The vessel arrived in Australia last month as well to complete a “scheduled, monthlong maintenance period” before returning next year to establish SRF-West, according to the Pentagon.
“They’ll return at the end of next year and establish their first rotational force there,” Cavanaugh said. “These aren’t just milestones, we’re really building a capacity and a capability there that’s going to benefit all three of our nations. At the same time, we’re accelerating innovation to expand our undersea advantage.”
Cavanaugh’s comments also come after the US, UK, and Australia concluded a naval exercise off the coast of California dubbed Maritime Big Play, which the UK’s Royal Navy described as the three countries’ “largest ever demonstration of uncrewed and autonomous technology” in support of AUKUS Pillar II. In particular, the Royal Navy said that the drill aimed to capitalize on more than 40 technologies spanning from manned, unmanned, and “multi-domain autonomous” systems” from the three countries.
Additionally, the US Navy said in a news release the exercise’s objective was to “achieve milestones in integrating mature robotics and autonomous systems within AUKUS coalition maritime operations.”

articles.title: Instead of stockpiling small attack drones, Army looking to simply buy new ones
articles.snippet: “It’s literally fly it as close as you can between those two fence posts because you might have to hit a high value target that way. And, if you crash 10 of them until you can get [number] 11 through, do it,” Army Material Command’s Jon Strzelec told Breaking Defense.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — As the Pentagon has been making a major effort to spread small drones across the force, logical questions have emerged about how the Pentagon plans to store these systems and how much money it will take to maintain and update them.
The solution, it turns out, is simpler than anyone could have expected: fly them “until they break,” according to one Army official.
“The Army had told us right away when we started this that none of this stuff’s getting stored on shelves because the iteration cycle is so much that we have to manufacture to deliver, not to stock,” Jon Strzelec, advanced manufacturing lead for small drones at Army Materiel Command, told Breaking Defense during an October interview.
At the core of the challenge is the reality that these drones become oboslete quickly. In Ukraine, Strzelec said, Russia can come up with a countermeasure for a new drone within 72 hours, forcing Kyiv to continue to upgrade and iterate on its designs. Subcomponents like the software, the circuit cards, the radio sets and cameras are all vulnerable to counters and need to be swapped out quickly.
“For us to take a drone off the shelf and take it apart, pull a card out, put a new card in it, flash the software, it’s cheaper in the assembly line process just to make a new one,” he later added.
Instead of using the word “sustain,” he added, the word for these smaller drones is “replace.”
The Pentagon is moving out on several efforts to buy new, small drones through efforts like the Drome Dominance program – a gauntlet-style competition billed as an avenue for spending $1 billion over two years – and broad plans to spend nearly $55 billion on its replacement for the Biden-era Replicator initiative that is called the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group (DAWG).
After gleaning observations from Ukraine, Army soldiers are expected to be a top consumer weapons with a mandate from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for every squad to be outfitted with them.
As of the interview, the Army was in the process of receiving 10,000 of the first 30,000 small drones out of the Drone Dominance Gauntlet 1, Strzelec said. Those drones will be sent to units for training, just like the Army does with equipment like M16s, Humvees and gas masks. The entire point is for soldiers to figure out how to train with them and use them in combat, not for them to sit on a shelf.
“It’s not just go crash in a tree and smack a high five,” Strzelec said. “It’s literally fly it as close as you can between those two fence posts because you might have to hit a high value target that way. And, if you crash 10 of them until you can get [number] 11 through, do it.”
“They’re practicing, they’re training but as they break, we’re not sustaining them,” he said separately.
James Slider, CEO of Performance Drone Works, told Breaking Defense that this Army plan to train with smaller drones solves the stockpile challenge he and others had been mulling over, especially given that on the “fast side of innovation cycle is three months” for these weapons.
Strzelec’s comments also fit into a larger concept outlined by Air Force Col. Dustin Thomas, the head of the Defense Contract Management Agency’s Unmanned Systems – Experimental (US-X) Command, in a trio of essays published by Breaking Defense. In those pieces, Thomas argued that the Pentagon needs to consistently be iterating and not be afraid to destroy these small systems, potentially to the rune of crashing 100,000 a year in order to better learn how they work.
Larger Systems, Different Plans
However, Strzelec was quick to note that what works for smaller systems may not be as applicable to slightly larger systems.
For some drones in group two category (21 to 55 lbs) that may be more expensive, and used to fly higher for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions or delivery operations, those will likely be sustained and used for longer.
“Mission set will dictate when we’re going to be using drones multiple times and as you change mission, you change cost, and so cost is going to be the driver of which ones are throwaways and which ones aren’t,” Strzelec added.
Strzelec’s comments will likely be welcomed by analysts, several of whom have told Breaking Defense in recent months that they are concerned the Pentagon is rushing to buy large quantities of systems without a clear plan for how to manage them long term.
Joe Costa, a former Pentagon official and currently the director of the Forward Defense program of the Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security at the Atlantic Council, recently told Breaking Defense the Pentagon should be “unquestionably” building out a sustainment plan given how much money it’s planning to spend.
“Who’s going to sustain them? Where are they going to be sustained? Is it going to be on the front lines?” he said.“The general challenge here is we think of drones very commonly now as attritiable. We use them, and then we’re going to let them go away. But some of the more advanced ones, you do want to come back to us.”
Erin Dumbacher, a former Pentagon official and currently with the Council on Foreign Relations, echoed similar questions and questioned the department’s plan for when components and software became obsolete.

articles.title: Cry ‘drone,’ and let slip the fruit flies of war
articles.snippet: The US military should focus on building drones that evolve so quickly an adversary’s defenses become obsolete before they can be deployed, two Air Force officers argue.
articles.full_text:
Scientists study fruit flies for a simple reason: they reproduce fast. As a result, researchers can change the environment and observe 25 generations of fruit flies each year.
Drones are the fruit flies of warfare, and their rapid evolution offers the military the chance to do something extraordinary: deliberately accelerate adaptation so that cheap changes on our side force expensive ones on theirs.
Traditional weapons take years, even decades, to develop and then remain in service for generations. Drones in every domain can evolve in weeks. Their radios, sensors, software, payloads, propulsion and even structures can change at different rates. In under a year, a drone can morph in both shape and function.
The clearest example is currently unfolding in the skies over Ukraine. Early in the war, Russia purchased and quickly employed simple Iranian Shahed drones with piston engines and a satellite receiver for navigation. It called them Gerans and within months, licensed the design and began building their own. Russian forces quickly began using them in inexpensive long-range attacks against Ukraine. Ukraine responded with electronic warfare to jam the satellite receiver and disrupt navigation. Russia countered with receivers designed to resist jamming. As Ukrainian jamming improved, the Geran grew new antennas in different patterns.
Ukraine also got better at tracking and shooting down Gerans. Russia added cameras and communications that allowed operators to see what the drones saw and redirect them in flight. Ukraine began using cheap interceptor drones to hunt them. Russia answered with speed — it first flew an Iranian jet-powered variant, the Shahed-238, then built its own Geran-3 by fitting the same airframe with a Chinese turbojet. The shortcut had a drawback: at twice the speed, the old Iranian airframe couldn’t take the G-loads. So, Russia did what it had previously avoided and redesigned the aircraft itself, producing the Geran-4 and Geran-5 and retooling its factories to build them. By August 2026 it had stopped making the Geran-3 altogether.
Ukraine had pushed reported interception rates against propeller-driven Gerans above 90 percent. Against the jet-powered models, the rate reportedly fell to around 60 percent. Since the jets fly higher, above cheap defenses like gun trucks and shoulder fired missiles, they drove Ukraine to generate fighter sorties and fire missiles it cannot spare, including scarce missiles.
In only a few years, the Geran family incorporated new navigation, communications, payloads, propulsion and airframe designs. Each Ukrainian response changed the threat environment. The Geran evolved to survive in it. Ukraine is now testing faster interceptors to catch them.
The pressure which drove the Geran’s evolution came from intense combat. But the American military doesn’t need to wait for an enemy to supply that pressure: it can provide its own, in training and test events where operators choose where to apply selection pressure, aiming it at a problem instead of merely surviving it.
The fruit fly comparison is not perfect, of course. Unlike with biological organisms, drones don’t reproduce or mutate by themselves — operators, engineers, manufacturers and military organizations decide which designs survive and continue to compete. But the underlying pattern is similar: short generations, variation, selection pressure, inheritance and recombination.
Scientists use fruit flies to understand biological processes that extend beyond flies themselves, since living organisms share a surprising amount of DNA. The military could use drones in a similar way by experimenting with technologies, interfaces, manufacturing and acquisition processes that also govern more complex weapon systems. While modeling and simulation can help, nothing beats physical experimentation when you are looking for the unexpected.
Today, the military generally tests systems to determine whether they meet requirements and to discover problems before combat. In competition-based acquisitions such as the Drone Dominance Program Gauntlets, testing helps select the best system. The program iterates but rewards the best drone rather than the teams that can produce successive generations the fastest.
However, the military could use testing for another purpose: to deliberately drive technological evolution. Pick several drone problems and give multiple teams twelve months to produce four generations. Every three months, change the threat environment. Introduce an interceptor, jam the GPS or change the mission. Some changes should be unexpected. Give the teams the results, let them adapt and repeat.
The initial experiment could involve tens or hundreds of drones per generation, rather than replacing an entire operational inventory every quarter. Each generation should produce a limited batch that operators can actually test and use, while demonstrating a credible path to larger-scale manufacturing.
Four generations in a year is, admittedly, an ambitious starting point, intended to expose the limits of the entire adaptation process. Whether three months is achievable is one of the questions the experiment should answer. But because the US — thankfully — is not in a Ukraine scenario, pushing the limits on what seems plausible is the best way to force rapid evolution.
In a recent article for Breaking Defense, I argued that the military should crash 100,000 drones a year in training. Even a small share of those flights could be chained into successive generations with the results of one becoming the starting point for the next. The military would learn which technologies — and which teams — keep producing useful, scalable solutions as the environment shifts. A team with the best drone in generation one could lose by generation four to a different team with a better process for adapting and manufacturing every three months. Russia pays for its adaptation in combat losses; we can pay for ours in training crashes.
The experiments should measure the time required for every stage of a generation. While a drone may be designed and prototyped in a week, the testing, manufacturing, contracting, delivery and training could take much longer. If all that takes a year, it means the generation took a year, no matter how fast the prototype came together. These experiments would reveal which parts of the overall system slow adaptation, and those are the processes which should be redesigned.
This is where the idea becomes a weapon. Once a military learns how to shorten the time between generations, it can study which changes force expensive responses from an opponent. The goal would be to identify which adaptations would be inexpensive to add but expensive and time-consuming for an adversary to counter: a software change that forces the adversary to change hardware; a hardware change that forces a system redesign; a system redesign that forces an overhaul of the adversary’s factories.
A military that can reliably field new generations faster than its adversary can respond gets to decide where that adversary spends its money, its engineers and its factory capacity. Ukraine spent years developing a layered defense against propeller Gerans. A change in propulsion to a commercial Chinese turbojet, then a new airframe built around it, rendered much of that layer irrelevant, forcing Ukraine back onto its most expensive interceptors. The military needs to figure out which of its own adaptations would do the same.
Imagine being an American adversary. You have finally developed a countermeasure to an American drone. Your engineers have solved the problem. Your factories are beginning to build the solution at scale. Your military is developing tactics and learning to use it. But the Americans are already two generations ahead with upgrades that your countermeasure may not defeat. Do you continue to produce the countermeasure? Redesign it? Or abandon your investment and start again?
And now, imagine that happening over and over again. An adversary could impose the same problem on the United States. The American military needs to learn how to create this advantage before an opponent does. And it can start by treating drones like fruit flies.
Col. Dustin “Whiz” Thomas is the Commander of the Defense Contract Management Agency’s Special Programs Command. He previously commanded DCMA’s Unmanned Systems–Experimental Command (US-X), where he led the Department of War’s Blue List program. He founded Game of Drones and previously led Black Phoenix, an initiative demonstrating the rapid design, manufacture and flight of unmanned aircraft. His work focuses on defense innovation, adaptive manufacturing and accelerating the fielding of emerging technologies.
Maj. Aubry J. Eaton, USAF, is an acquisition and intelligence professional currently serving as a Department of the Air Force Strategic Policy Fellow. His work has previously appeared in Joint Force Quarterly and War on the Rocks.
The views expressed in this article are those of the authors and do not reflect the official policy or position of the Department of the Air Force, the Defense Contract Management Agency, the Department of War or the U.S. Government.

articles.title: Rethinking the pipeline for critical defense electronics
articles.snippet: [Sponsored] Closing the gap for space systems, EW and counter-UAS production.
articles.full_text:
Military necessity to respond to emerging threats in near-real time is putting pressure on a traditional acquisition process built on lengthy Research, Development, Test, and Evaluation (RDT&E) cycles before a new capability can pass to warfighters. Nowhere is that more apparent than in radio frequency (RF) technology, where rapidly changing electronic warfare (EW) threats, new communications requirements for command and control, and expanding missions are forcing the defense industrial base to deliver more capability in less time.
The challenge extends beyond designing faster processors or more powerful RF amplifiers. Defense electronics must meet increasingly demanding size, weight, power, and thermal constraints for autonomous platforms, for example, while remaining adaptable to new waveforms, frequencies, and operational requirements. At the same time, supply-chain limitations and production schedules are the determining factor in how quickly those systems reach the warfighter.
For companies supplying electronics to prime contractors, the answer increasingly involves adapting proven designs rather than developing every capability from scratch. That approach reduces technical risk, shortens qualification timelines, and makes it easier to integrate new functionality into existing platforms.
“We don’t have time to field an entire platform, come back, see what happens, go do another one,” said Lorne Graves, senior vice president and chief technology officer at Frontgrade Technologies [Frontgrade]. “Those days are gone.”
Adapting to threats faster than traditional acquisition allows
As mentioned, there’s a mismatch between the pace of technological change and the time required to develop, qualify, and produce military electronics. For RF systems used in EW, tactical communications, radar, and space applications, requirements can change considerably during a traditional acquisition cycle. An architecture developed for one threat environment may need to accommodate different frequencies, waveforms, or operating conditions by the time it is fielded.
That puts a premium on adaptable hardware and designs that allow new capabilities to be introduced without replacing an entire subsystem.
“The time it takes to respond to these threats means that you wouldn’t field the platform,” said Graves. “The architecture better have adaptability to be able to change and counter those threats.”
Such adaptability doesn’t come from pursuing highly customized solutions for every requirement. Rather, the solution is increasingly the application of commercially developed capabilities and existing qualified designs “to effectively get a good enough solution without having to create a very bespoke solution to meet a very narrow set of requirements,” said Jack Kilian, senior vice president and chief growth officer for Frontgrade.
In practice, that could mean beginning with a design that already meets 80 percent of a program’s requirements, then adapting particular functions, interfaces, or performance characteristics. It could also involve qualification by “similarity”, using evidence from an existing design to reduce the testing needed for a related configuration, according to Kilian.
For the military, the advantage is not simply a shorter procurement timeline as it facilitates the bringing of evolved capabilities to the field sooner while preserving a path for subsequent upgrades as the threat changes.
Supply chain resilience becomes part of the mission
The same emphasis on speed is changing how electronics suppliers manage manufacturing capacity. RF systems depend on specialized semiconductors, materials, and mechanical components that can be difficult to source. Gallium nitride, widely used in high-performance RF applications, illustrates the challenge because of supply-chain exposure involving the raw gallium required for its production.
Kilian noted the concentration of gallium production in China and the export restrictions that have increased concerns about access to critical materials. Bearings, magnets, and other components can also create lengthy production delays.
Frontgrade is addressing those risks through multiple sourcing, strategic inventories of critical parts, and greater internal manufacturing capability. The company is qualifying additional suppliers to reduce dependence on individual manufacturers, and maintaining stocks of components used across multiple product lines so production teams can respond more quickly without committing inventory to a single, specialized design. Standardizing certain components across products can substantially shorten delivery schedules.
“It can significantly pull in these lead times from beyond 52 weeks to below 26 weeks in many cases for these deliverables,” said Kilian. That means, for example, that Frontgrade can get critical hardware and electronics into a prime contractor’s hands for integration onto a communications satellite.
Integrating the electronics backbone
Frontgrade’s advanced RF capabilities have expanded through the addition of Aethercomm (acquired in 2023), IDSI (the Defense Solutions division of Crescend Technologies acquired in 2025), and Tricom Research (2025), complementing its existing portfolio of antennas, radiation-hardened electronics, processing, and power technologies.
Together, those capabilities cover a substantial portion of the signal chain from RF signal acquisition and conditioning through conversion, digital processing, and storage – whether they be individual components or larger integrated systems.
“Our prime customers are looking for partners that can effectively deliver integrated subsystem solutions that are ready to layer their application software on top of it,” said Kilian, noting in that arrangement that suppliers like Frontgrade can deliver hardware together with the middleware and application programming interfaces needed to support higher-level software integration.
Customers can purchase components to build their own boards, obtain board-level subsystems, or use more complete integrated systems that already combine RF, digital conversion, processing, and storage. The objective is to let prime contractors concentrate on the application and mission requirements rather than having to integrate every underlying electronic component themselves.
For military users, the implications extend across multiple mission areas. EW, radar, SATCOM, and counter-UAS systems operate across different frequency bands, but they share the need for efficient RF amplification, signal conditioning, and reliable performance under demanding environmental conditions.
The company’s acquired RF capabilities from the acquisitions mentioned above include technologies with a storied history in counter-improvised explosive device (IED) systems dating to the early 2000s – particularly the Counter Radio-Controlled Improvised Explosive Device Electronic Warfare (CREW) system that jammed RF signals that set off IEDs. That heritage also informs applications involving counter-UAS and other EW missions.
Another important requirement for today’s military electronics is delivering greater RF power from smaller packages while controlling thermal loads. Frontgrade provides efficient power amplifiers for small spaces that operate in high-thermal environments. Those attributes’ constraints are especially significant in space, where spacecraft cannot rely on the cooling approaches commonly available in terrestrial data centers and communications facilities.
The result is an engineering tradeoff in which power output, efficiency, packaging, and thermal performance is considered together rather than optimized independently.
Building adaptability into the hardware
The next step is making RF electronics easier to modify after the initial system design has been completed. Graves distinguishes between scalability, which generally involves expanding an existing capability, and extensibility, which allows proven technology to be adapted for different operating environments and mission requirements.
Common design elements developed for space, counter-UAS, and EW applications can serve as starting points for related systems. Using previously qualified modules can reduce development effort and enable suppliers to meet more demanding deployment schedules.
For example, that philosophy informs the design of Frontgrade’s power amplifiers. Rather than treating an amplifier as fixed hardware with a single operating configuration, Frontgrade is incorporating telemetry, health monitoring, and software-controlled features that allow performance to be adjusted to changing requirements. Those features support changes in power efficiency and waveform characteristics without necessarily requiring a hardware replacement.
Graves described these devices as “smart” power amplifiers, with controls intended to make the RF chain more responsive to operational requirements. The distinction becomes critical for equipment deployed in space as physical access to satellites is generally unavailable, making software adaptability considerably more important.
With having software-controlled RF capabilities, operators can adapt to interference and maintain communications links needed to deliver information to warfighters. The goal is to preserve the usefulness of existing hardware as threats and mission requirements evolve rather than treating every new requirement as a reason to redesign the system.

articles.title: DoD pushes out 3 loans totaling $450M to bolster US space companies
articles.snippet: One industry source told Breaking Defense that the reason for the spate of new loan announcements is that the Pentagon “needed to finalize loans by the end of the fiscal year.”
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON ― The Defense Department’s Office of Strategic Capital has recently announced three loans, worth a total of $450 million, to US space firms to bolster launch and space monitoring capacities.
The most recent of these was a $150 million loan to Rocket Lab, announced on Monday, to help the firm “increase the flight rate of its reusable Neutron rocket beyond first launch to meet growing commercial and national security demand for access to space.”
Rocket Lab last month confirmed that Neutron’s first launch has been delayed from late this year until sometime next year. The firm originally had planned to launch the medium-lift rocket in 2024, then pushed that date back to late 2025.
Another $150 million loan was awarded on Oct. 26 to startup Stoke Space to help it build a second launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida for its planned Nova reusable rocket. Stoke originally had hoped to launch Nova in 2025, but now is planning lift off in March 2027.
Those two awards attest to the Pentagon’s growing unease about a potential gap in the availability of space launch vehicles post 2028, when SpaceX will stop flying commercial payloads on Falcon 9. An Oct. 29 report by Quilty Space found a likely shortfall of at least 150 launches between now and 2030, including for military payloads as Space Force demand increases.
Both Rocket Lab and Stoke were added in March 2025 to the Space Force’s pool of potential launch providers under the service’s National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 3 Lane 1 program, which covers launches to easier to reach orbits, payloads with less mass, and missions that are not absolute must-goes.
The Pentagon also announced on Nov. 4 a loan worth $150 million to space monitoring firm LeoLabs to “accelerate the deployment of critical radar infrastructure and advanced decision science software,” in particular, deployment of the company’s new Scout mobile radar.
According to a Nov. 5 LeoLabs announcement, the award will help expand its domestic radar manufacturing capacity, including completion of “two large-scale manufacturing facilities by 2028.”
One industry source told Breaking Defense that the reason for the spate of new loan announcements is that the Pentagon “needed to finalize loans by the end of the fiscal year” and thus “have been rolling them out on a regular cadence since.” (While fiscal 2026 officially ended Sept. 30, DoD contract announcements often don’t come until after actual awards to allow for official paperwork to be completed.)
This spate of year-end activity by the Office of Strategic Capital includes loans for non-space related activities as well.
For example, DoD on Nov. 2 announced a “loan commitment of up to $450 million” to startup drone maker Neros to support the firm’s “planned expansion of vertically integrated domestic manufacturing capacity” to produce dual-use sUAS [small unmanned aircraft systems] platforms, ground control systems, and critical components like motors, radios, flight electronics, sensors, and batteries.”
And on Nov. 5, a $75 million loan to Halo Industries was announced to help the California-based firm scale production of its “innovative Silicon Carbide (SiC) semiconductor wafers.”
Like all loans granted by the Office of Strategic Capital, the three space company loans are “conditional,” requiring a process of due diligence about the grantee’s finances. In addition, the loans require a matching investment of company capital.
The office was created by DoD in 2022 under the Office of the Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, and subsequently was authorized by Congress to run a pilot investment program in the FY24 National Defense Authorization Act to run through FY28.
According to a September report by the Congressional Research Service, the Office of Strategic Capital’s remit includes both “direct debt financing for companies and the financing of venture capital, private equity, and other investment funds,” as well as “loans and loan guarantees to third-party investment funds.”
Further, the report explained that for FY26, Congress appropriated $97.8 million for its “capital assistance pilot program,” designed to “subsidize up to $4.4 billion in loans, loan guarantees, and technical assistance.” The Office of Strategic Capital also received $2 million for FY26 through the defense-wide research, development, test, and evaluation (RDT&E) account.
The office put out its first notice of $984 million in direct loan funding availability on a “rolling basis” in September 2024, accompanied by a Federal Register notice that listed 34 categories of dual-use technology for potential investment. While the office is focused largely on microelectronics and computer-related tech, three of these are space specific: “space launch; spacecraft; and space-enabled services and equipment.” Several more are space adjacent, including optical communications, sensor hardware and solar power.
The September CRS report added that the Pentagon’s FY27 budget request said the office would use $20 million in FY25 reconciliation funding for RDT&E activities during in FY26.
The FY27 request further includes $216 million in discretionary funding and $20 billion in mandatory funding for the Office of Strategic Capital’s capital assistance pilot program, as well as $19 million for the office’s RDT&E activities, CRS found.

articles.title: EU sets out $3.4B defense budget for 2027, boosts Ukraine spending
articles.snippet: The new fiscal uplift comes in the wake of Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy telling European leaders last month that “we need at least €70 billion more from you.”
articles.full_text:
BELFAST — The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union have agreed to a 2027 defense and security budget valued at €3.1 ($3.4 billion), the bloc announced, spurred by the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
“To step up to the challenge of the current geopolitical situation” next year’s annual budget includes “major support to Ukraine,” based on Ukraine Support Loan funding and the Ukraine Facility, according to an EU statement released today.
The Ukraine Support Loan funding for the year is listed at €650 million, a boost to the previously promised pool of €90 billion. (The Ukraine Facility is a separate mechanism designed to facilitates tens of billions of euros to Kyiv in grants and loans.)
The announcement comes a month after Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told European leaders that “we need at least €70 billion more from you” on top of the promised €90 billion in loans as the war with Russia looks set to enter its fifth year.
The UK’s Guardian newspaper reported that the EU appears to have heard Zelenskyy’s call, promising to dig up €45 billion with the remaining shortfall potentially made up by Canada and the UK. It wasn’t immediately clear how the recently announced budget plays into the proposed €45 billion, and a spokesperson for the bloc did not respond to a request for comment today.
The 2027 budget is the last from the EU’s existing Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), before members decide on a new version covering longer-term spending plans between 2028-2034.
Those discussions are reportedly already engulfed in geopolitical drama. The Financial Times reported that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned that he will block the future, multiyear budget, should any EU member states refuse to provide financial support for Ukraine. Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic previously opted out of the EU’s initial €90 billion loan. Those three nations and Bulgaria have also signaled that they won’t contribute to future lending.
“A collective commitment that all of us, without exception, will contribute fairly to closing [Ukraine’s financing] gap is an essential prerequisite for resolving this issue and for discussing any further matters, particularly those with financial implications,” Merz purportedly wrote in a letter sent to European Council President António Costa, per the business news outlet.
Outside of how future budget negotiations play out, the EU’s own budget preparation documents make clear that maintaining monetary support for the war-torn nation, while in parallel reacting to other regional or international events has become an increasingly difficult task.
“The EU budget has shown versatility, but it also demonstrated the limits of its current architecture, thus requiring a mid-term revision to adequately address additional needs for Ukraine, migration and its root causes, responding to the crises in the Middle East, reinforcing our capacity to respond to natural disasters, and support for boosting investments in critical technologies and defence,” noted a European Commission statement of estimates for FY2027.

articles.title: Shipping giant Maersk says recent cyber incident affected legacy system
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The incident is the latest in a string of attacks on ports and other shipping organizations worldwide, with Brazil’s largest port hit with ransomware last week.
articles.full_text:
Shipping giant Maersk says recent cyber incident affected legacy system
Danish shipping company Maersk said threat actors gained access to a “legacy system from a previous acquisition,” but said the incident does not impact other parts of the firm.
The incident affecting Maersk, one of the largest shipping companies in the world with a 2025 revenue of $54 billion, is the latest in a string of attacks on ports and other shipping organizations worldwide. Brazil’s largest port was hit with ransomware last week and is still struggling to restore systems through Thursday.
Maersk said its findings suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed, and it does not anticipate disruptions for customers. “The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI,” the company said.
Maersk provided few details on the attack but the statement came three days after the WhiteArmor ransomware gang claimed it attacked LF Logistics. The Hong-Kong based transportation and logistics company was acquired by Maersk in 2022.
The ransomware gang claimed it stole 100GB of data from LF Logistics and demanded $5 million in 30 days. The stolen data allegedly includes information on LF Logistics drivers, warehouses, customers and more.
Maersk, which has previously dealt with ransomware affecting company systems as well as specific port operations, is not the only shipping organization to be dealing with a cyber incident.
An attack on Brazil’s Santos Port Authority — one of the largest in South America — began last Friday and caused a power outage, eventually leading to significant delays in loading and unloading cargo while also forcing officials to conduct route scheduling and billing services manually.
The Santos Port Authority said on Thursday that it has been able to recover about 70% of its systems through backups. Brazil’s Federal Police are now investigating the attack.
Ports in the U.S., Europe and Asia have been repeatedly targeted by ransomware gangs over the last five years as many shift to incorporate digital operations. In 2024, the Port of Seattle refused to pay a ransom to cybercriminals that caused issues at the city’s airport and seaport ahead of the Labor Day holiday.

articles.title: European authorities take down SteaIC malware servers for second time this year
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: German authorities on Thursday said investigators traced the rebuilt network to the  Virtualine bulletproof hosting provider, seized by the FBI in October, with the assistance of police in Frankfurt and the Dutch National High Tech Crime Unit.
articles.full_text:
European authorities take down SteaIC malware servers for second time this year
European police dismantled more than 100 servers used by the StealC password-stealing malware this week, marking the second such takedown after an initial crackdown in June.
German authorities on Thursday said investigators traced the rebuilt network to the Virtualine bulletproof hosting provider, seized by the FBI in October, with the assistance of police in Frankfurt and the Dutch National High Tech Crime Unit.
Europol said a wider international operation this week saw law enforcement agencies and private sector partners disrupt 235 servers and 257 domains used by StealC alongside the Gootloader and CastleRAT malware.
Investigators uncovered copies of around 6.4 million stolen login credentials from more than 40,000 victims obtained by this malware. People have been encouraged to visit politie.nl/checkyourhack and haveibeenpwned.com to see if they were impacted, and to find out what to do if they were.
No arrests, cryptocurrency seizures or criminal charges accompanied the action.
The authorities and Microsoft previously announced in June they dismantled hundreds of servers and domains linked to StealC and other malware tools. At the time, investigators restricted access to €41 million ($47 million) in cryptocurrency.
Police from nine countries, including Germany, the Netherlands, Britain and the United States, took part in the latest operation, which aims to target the most significant tools used by cybercriminals globally.
Carsten Meywirth, the head of the cybercrime department at Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office, said the move marked the agency’s “long-term strategy and a high-speed approach” to tackling cybercrime.
“Even technically skilled and well-organized cybercriminals must expect coordinated international investigations,” said Meywirth.
“We have once again demonstrated that, together with our international partners and private cybersecurity companies, we can neutralize even seemingly untouchable malware. Anyone who rebuilds their infrastructure after police action leaves new leads that we will pursue.”

articles.title: ConnectWise investigates ScreenConnect breaches after reports of incidents at nearly 50 organizations
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Abuse of an independent third-party tool led to breaches at ScreenConnect customers, confirmed the software's maker, ConnectWise. Cybersecurity researchers had spotted intrusions at nearly 50.
articles.full_text:
ConnectWise investigates ScreenConnect breaches after reports of incidents at nearly 50 organizations
IT management software company ConnectWise said it is investigating reports of unauthorized access to its customers following reports from multiple cybersecurity firms that almost 50 organizations had been breached through the company’s ScreenConnect tool.
Late on Wednesday evening, ConnectWise said it believes the activity is related to the abuse of an independent third-party extension installed in customer environments. The tool, RMM+, is an extension for ConnectWise ScreenConnect that allows external management tools to automate and control remote sessions through an API.
“We identified approximately 400 partner environments with at least one independently developed third-party extension from the RMM+ family installed. Their presence alone does not establish compromise,” the company said.
“These extensions provide an API capable of executing remote commands. Access to that API is protected by a passphrase configured by the partner during setup.”
The Tampa-based company told customers that threat actors were deploying additional remote-access software and also saw “potential compromise of technician workstations during interactive connections to affected devices. “
The company disabled RMM+ in the 400 customer environments and urged customers with on-premises systems to disable it themselves because ConnectWise cannot do it for them. All customers should verify that RMM+ is disabled.
Customers should also be wary of any ScreenConnect connections to suspected compromised devices, ConnectWise added.
“Disabling extensions and resetting credentials alone may not remove unauthorized software, persistence mechanisms, or access already established on endpoints,” the company said, warning of unusual sign-ins and repeated login failures.
ConnectWise initially said it identified five different third-party extensions that may be associated with the malicious activity but later traced it back to RMM+.
Compromised credentials?
The advisories that prompted ConnectWise to act came after cybersecurity firm Huntress said it saw 288 affected endpoints across 48 organizations targeted within 90 minutes. Huntress incident responders found commands tied to RMM+ across several ScreenConnect systems and confirmed that ConnectWise disabled RMM+ alongside four other third-party extensions.
“Huntress hasn’t seen evidence of a new vulnerability, but it’s still unclear how the attacker got panel access. Current telemetry points to compromised credentials or hijacked operator sessions to gain initial access, but Huntress’ researchers will update when they know more,” a Huntress spokesperson said.
In several attacks, the threat actors used compromised systems to create persistent backdoors and used infected endpoints to spread malware throughout a network when a technician connected to that compromised endpoint.
ScreenConnect is used widely by managed service providers that run company IT infrastructure and end-user systems.
Huntress and several other researchers said the attack campaign may be tied to a ConnectWise vulnerability discovered in September — CVE-2026-84869. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency warned that it was being exploited in September.
Blackpoint Cyber researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal told Recorded Future News that they were able to reverse engineer the toolkit the attackers used in the recent ScreenConnect attacks and said it involves the exploitation of CVE-2026-84869.
Both researchers noted that they tested the toolkit against a fully patched ScreenConnect client and confirmed the patch works — meaning those exploited were likely unpatched.
“Our testing confirmed that the exploit targets CVE-2026-84869 and that the existing patch successfully blocks it,” Decker and Beal added.
“But the toolkit also includes capabilities to hijack authenticated operator sessions and use legitimate ScreenConnect management features to push malicious code. Patching addresses the known exploit, but it doesn't eliminate the risks associated with a compromised operator session. Organizations need to protect those sessions and put additional safeguards around high-impact administrative actions.”
ConnectWise has repeatedly faced attacks from both nation-states and cybercriminals in recent years. Last month, Microsoft warned that a Chinese government-aligned hacking group used automated tools to carry out a supply chain attack on ConnectWise.
Chinese government groups have repeatedly targeted ScreenConnect since 2024 because of its widespread use across U.S. businesses and government agencies.
